summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module with managed objects for the Fabric Address Manager of a Fibre Channel network. Network management tools can use it to monitor how addresses are handed out. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4439 defines the SNMP managed objects for the Fabric Address Manager, the part of a Fibre Channel switch that gives out addresses and keeps the fabric configured. It covers the settings and counters of each switch, the database of domain IDs, the addresses assigned in each area, a cache of recently released addresses, and the notifications and commands that report and trigger a fabric rebuild.

subtitle: The managed objects that let a network manager see and control how a Fibre Channel fabric hands out addresses.

tldr.problem: A Fibre Channel fabric hands out short address identifiers dynamically, and one switch in the fabric decides who gets which domain ID. Without managed objects for that job, a network manager cannot see which switch holds which domain, how many addresses are free, or why a fabric is not settling down.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module with a main table holding the address manager's settings and counters for every switch and fabric, plus tables for interfaces, for the port identifiers assigned in each area, for the domain database, and for a cache of recently released identifiers. Read-write objects can set a switch's domain ID, its priority and ask it to rebuild the fabric.
tldr.outcome: The result is that the address manager of a Fibre Channel switch can be monitored and driven over SNMP, with the module registered under mib-2 and the states of the manager reported as a single enumerator. The document is explicit that the write-capable objects can disturb a running fabric and need protection.

today: RFC 4439 is a Proposed Standard from March 2006 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It defines two MIB modules: T11-TC-MIB for textual conventions used by other T11 MIBs, and T11-FC-FABRIC-ADDR-MGR-MIB for the Fabric Address Manager itself. It builds on the Fibre Channel Management MIB, which is a T11 document rather than an RFC, and on the Fibre Channel switch fabric standards FC-SW-3 and FC-SW-4.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in the Internet community, and in particular it describes managed objects for information related to a Fibre Channel network's Fabric Address Manager. That name refers to the functionality of acquiring Domain_IDs as specified in the Fibre Channel switch fabric standard FC-SW-3, and of managing Fibre Channel Identifiers as specified in FC-FS.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, and MIB objects are generally accessed through SNMP. The objects in this memo are defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information, and the module is compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

The document defines two MIB modules. T11-TC-MIB defines textual conventions that might also be useful in other MIBs defined by T11, and it is registered at mib-2 136. T11-FC-FABRIC-ADDR-MGR-MIB holds the managed objects for the Fabric Address Manager and is registered at mib-2 137. IANA has made those two MIB OID assignments.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 4439 defines the management objects that let a network manager see and control how a Fibre Channel fabric hands out addresses. It defines two MIB modules: one with shared type definitions, and one with the objects for the address manager itself.

sections.title: A Short Overview of Fibre Channel
sections.content:
Fibre Channel is logically a bidirectional point-to-point serial data channel, structured for high performance. It provides a general transport vehicle for higher-level protocols such as SCSI command sets, the High-Performance Parallel Interface data framing, IP, IEEE 802.2 and others.

Physically, Fibre Channel is an interconnection of multiple communication points, called N_Ports, interconnected either by a switching network, called a Fabric, or by a point-to-point link. A Fibre Channel node consists of one or more N_Ports, and a Fabric may consist of multiple Interconnect Elements, some of which are switches. An N_Port connects to the Fabric through a port on a switch called an F_Port. When multiple FC nodes are connected to a single switch port through an Arbitrated Loop topology, that port is called an FL_Port and the nodes' ports are NL_Ports. A switch port that is interconnected to another switch port through an Inter-Switch Link is called an E_Port, and a B_Port connects a bridge device with an E_Port, providing a subset of E_Port functionality.

Many Fibre Channel components, including the Fabric, each node and most ports, have globally-unique names, typically formatted as World Wide Names, and these are expected to be persistent across agent and unit resets.

Fibre Channel frames contain 24-bit address identifiers that identify the frame's source and destination ports, and each FC port has both an address identifier and a World Wide Name. When a Fabric is in use, the address identifiers are dynamically assigned by a switch. Each octet of a 24-bit address represents a level in an address hierarchy, with a Domain_ID being the highest level of that hierarchy.

Each switch in a Fabric is assigned one or more unique Domain_IDs using a two-step process. First, one switch, called the Principal Switch, is selected from the switches of the Fabric. Then the Principal Switch assigns Domain_IDs to the other switches. Address assignment within a domain is performed by the switch to which that Domain_ID was granted.
sections.plainLanguage: Fibre Channel connects storage nodes through a network of switches, called a fabric. Each port has a persistent worldwide name and a short address that the fabric hands out. The highest part of that address is a domain ID, and one switch in the fabric, the principal switch, gives domain IDs to the others.

sections.title: Relationship to Other MIBs
sections.content:
The first standardized MIB for Fibre Channel, RFC 2837, focused on Fibre Channel switches. It is being replaced by the more generic Fibre Channel Management MIB, which defines basic information for Fibre Channel hosts and switches, including extensions to the standard IF-MIB for Fibre Channel interfaces, and which specifies how the generic objects defined in the IF-MIB apply to Fibre Channel interfaces.

One constraint carries over from that MIB. An interface's ifIndex value must be unique within an SNMP context, irrespective of how many Fibre Channel management instances and how many Fibre Channel switches are instrumented within that SNMP context.

This document goes beyond the Fibre Channel Management MIB to cover the functionality in Fibre Channel switches that is used to manage fabric configuration, domains and addresses within a domain. It imports the management instance index, the switch index and the types for a domain ID and a name from that MIB, and the Fibre Channel interface index from the IF-MIB, so the two modules fit together under one management framework.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB builds on the Fibre Channel Management MIB, which holds the basic host and switch information, and on the standard interface MIB. This one covers the part that hands out addresses and keeps the fabric configured.

sections.title: The Layout of the MIB
sections.content:
Three identifiers sit underneath the tables. A Fibre Channel management instance is a separable managed instance of Fibre Channel functionality, and functionality may be grouped into instances in whatever way is most convenient for the implementation, for example one SNMP agent with several AgentX sub-agents, each implementing a different instance. The index fcmInstanceIndex identifies it. The Switch Index, fcmSwitchIndex, identifies one Fibre Channel switch among those managed by the same management instance. The Fabric Index, t11FamFabricIndex, is an arbitrary integer that identifies a particular Fabric within one or more physical infrastructures; in a Fabric conformant to FC-SW-3, where there is always exactly one Fabric in a single physical infrastructure, its value is always 1, while FC-SW-4 supports several Fabrics, each with its own management instrumentation, operating within one or more physical infrastructures.

Because a port of a switch may be connected to several Fabrics, the switch index is listed before the fabric index whenever both appear in the same INDEX clause, which simplifies a query about all the Fabrics a single switch is connected to.

The objects are divided into six groups. The t11FamGroup group holds basic information about the Fabric Address Manager within a switch, including its configuration parameters that are per-interface. The t11FamDatabaseGroup group holds information about which switches are assigned to which domains. The t11FamAreaGroup group holds information about which port IDs have been assigned within the areas of the local domain. The t11FamCacheGroup group, which is conditionally mandatory, holds information about all the address identifier assignments that have recently been released, and is kept to support the concept of a preferred Domain_ID through a best-effort attempt at re-assigning the same identifiers. The t11FamCommandGroup group, which is optional, holds the objects used for initiating an operation on a Fabric, and the t11FamNotificationGroup group holds notifications of significant events concerning the address management functionality within a switch.
sections.plainLanguage: Every object is found by three identifiers: which management instance, which switch, and which fabric. The objects themselves sit in six groups, covering the address manager's own settings, the domain database, the areas, the cache of released addresses, commands and notifications.

sections.title: The Managed Objects and Their Tables
sections.content:
The main table, t11FamTable, holds the Fabric Address Manager parameters that can be configured and monitored in a Fibre Channel switch, with one row for each switch managed by a management instance and each Fabric known to that switch. Rows are implicitly created and removed as additional Fabrics are created and deleted, and the row is indexed by the management instance, the switch and the fabric.

The configurable objects in that row include the configured Domain_ID and the type of that Domain_ID, a flag for automatic reconfiguration, a flag for contiguous allocation, the switch's priority, the World Wide Names of the principal switch and of the local switch, the list of assigned area IDs, counters and gauges for the address identifiers granted, recovered, free, assigned and available, the running priorities, the state of the address manager, counters for principal switch selections, fabric builds and fabric reconfigurations, the Domain_ID in use, and flags for sticky behaviour, restart, notification control, enabling the manager and the fabric name.

Three more tables sit alongside it. The t11FamIfTable holds the per-interface configuration of the address manager, including the role of the inter-switch link, a flag for rejecting a reconfiguration request and a row status object. The t11FamAreaTable holds, for each area of the fabric, the area ID and the list of port IDs assigned within it, and each octet of the assigned area list is an index into it. The t11FamDatabaseTable holds all the information a switch has about the domains assigned in each fabric, that is, which switch currently holds each domain ID, named by its World Wide Name. The t11FamFcIdCacheTable holds the address identifiers the manager has recently released, with the maximum cache size given by t11FamMaxFcIdCacheSize, so that a switch can make a best-effort attempt at re-assigning the same identifier to the same port the next time it asks for one.
sections.plainLanguage: The main table has one row per switch and fabric, holding the settings and the counters. Three smaller tables hold the per-interface settings, the port identifiers assigned in each area, the domain IDs and who holds them, and the identifiers that were recently given back so they can be handed out again.

sections.title: The State of the Address Manager
sections.content:
One object reports where the address manager has got to, and its value is drawn from a set of twelve states described in Table 86 and Figure 15 of FC-SW-3. The value other stands for a switch in a state not represented by any of the others. Starting stands for a switch engaged in the process represented by the first row of that table, and unconfigured for a switch that requires operator input before it can begin that process. principalSwitchSelection stands for a switch engaged in the process of the second row, and domainIdDistribution for the third row. buildFabricPhase stands for a switch in state F0 of Figure 15 and reconfigureFabricPhase for state F1.

The remaining values describe a switch that has finished. stable means it has successfully completed the process of the third row and has at least one E_Port, and stableWithNoEports means it completed it but has no E_Ports. noDomains means it completed the process but failed to obtain a Domain_ID. disabled stands for any situation in which the corresponding instance of t11FamEnable is false, and unknown for a switch that is confused about what state it is in.
sections.plainLanguage: One object says where the address manager has got to, from starting and choosing a principal switch, through handing out domain IDs, to a stable state with or without external ports.

sections.title: Reconfiguring the Fabric
sections.content:
Two commands of the switch fabric internal link service matter here. Reconfigure Fabric, RCF, causes a complete reconfiguration of the fabric and may change the addresses allocated to a switch, so the Fibre Channel standard warns that it should be used with caution. Build Fabric, BF, lets the fabric attempt a reconfiguration without loss of or change of address, and it should be attempted before an RCF. Situations in which RCF may be appropriate include the resolution of overlapped domains, or the failure of a fabric reconfiguration initiated by a BF.

A fabric is prohibited from autonomously generating an RCF, but an outside administrative function may request a switch to generate one. The MIB is consistent with that rule, because it defines two objects with read-write access, t11FamAutoReconfigure and t11FamRestart, and setting them to the appropriate value is a means by which an outside administrative function may request an RCF.

t11FamAutoReconfigure determines how the switch responds to certain error conditions, such as the merging of two disjoint Fabrics that have overlapping Domain_ID lists. When the value is true the switch sends an RCF to rebuild the fabric, and when it is false the switch isolates the E_Ports on which the errors happened. t11FamRestart asks for a fabric reconfiguration directly: set to disruptive it generates an RCF, set to nonDisruptive it generates a BF, and noOp takes no action. The value read back is always noOp.

Two limits are worth noting. The compliance section of the MIB gives read-only as the minimum required support for those two objects. And the MIB serves only as a request: a successful SNMP SetRequest on them causes an RCF or BF to be sent, but SNMP cannot ensure that the underlying command succeeds.
sections.plainLanguage: Two objects can ask a switch to rebuild the fabric. One triggers a full reconfiguration, which can change addresses; the other asks for a gentler rebuild that keeps them. Both are only requests, and the standard wants a gentler rebuild to be tried first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of the managed objects have a read-write or read-create access clause, and may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Supporting SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The document lists what each writable object can do. The Domain_ID objects and the contiguous allocation flag change the address allocation policy. The restart and auto-reconfigure objects can cause a fabric reconfiguration, for instance on certain error conditions. The priority object affects which switch becomes the Principal Switch. The notification enable object turns a notification on or off, the per-interface reject flag changes the switch's behaviour on receipt of an RCF, and the row status object changes an interface configuration parameter.

Some of the readable objects may be sensitive too, so it is important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to them and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network with SNMP. The main table and the interface table hold the configuration, status and statistics of the address manager, while the area, database and cache tables hold information on currently assigned or recently released addresses.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Even where the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is no control over who on that network is allowed to read or change the objects in this module. The document therefore recommends using the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and does not recommend deploying earlier SNMP versions. It is then a customer or operator responsibility to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB module is properly configured to give access only to those principals that have legitimate rights to read or change them.
sections.plainLanguage: Several of these objects can disturb a running fabric, so writes to them need protection, and even reads can reveal information about which addresses are in use. The document recommends SNMPv3 with its authentication and privacy, and careful control of who may read or change each object.

items.label: other
items.desc: A switch in a state not represented by any of the other values.

items.label: starting
items.desc: Engaged in the first step of the fabric bring-up process.

items.label: unconfigured
items.desc: Needs operator input before it can begin the fabric bring-up process.

items.label: principalSwitchSelection
items.desc: Engaged in the second step, the choice of principal switch.

items.label: domainIdDistribution
items.desc: Engaged in the third step, the distribution of domain IDs.

items.label: buildFabricPhase
items.desc: A switch in state F0 of the fabric bring-up figure.

items.label: reconfigureFabricPhase
items.desc: A switch in state F1 of the fabric bring-up figure.

items.label: stable
items.desc: Completed the domain ID distribution step and has at least one E_Port.

items.label: stableWithNoEports
items.desc: Completed the domain ID distribution step but has no E_Ports.

items.label: noDomains
items.desc: Completed the domain ID distribution step but failed to obtain a Domain_ID.

items.label: disabled
items.desc: The address manager is disabled for that instance.

items.label: unknown
items.desc: The switch is confused about what state it is in.
